stories.title: Haze Returns: Malaysia's Air Turns Unhealthy in 30 Places
stories.headline_kid: Smoky air from forest fires in Indonesia has made the sky hazy and unhealthy in nearby Malaysia — and Singapore is keeping a close eye on the wind.
summary: Every year around this time, farmers and companies in Indonesia burn forests to clear land quickly and cheaply. This creates thick smoke called haze, which drifts with the wind to neighbouring countries like Malaysia and Singapore.

On Tuesday, Malaysia recorded 'unhealthy' air quality in about 30 areas, mostly along the west coast of Peninsular Malaysia and in parts of Sarawak. Air quality is measured using a number — the higher it goes, the dirtier and more harmful the air becomes to breathe.

Indonesia's President Prabowo Subianto has ordered that companies suspected of deliberately starting these fires have their business permits cancelled. Fires in Sumatra and Kalimantan have already burned about 85,000 hectares of land — that's roughly the size of 119,000 football fields!
Singapore's own air agency, NEA, is watching wind patterns closely. If the haze blows our way, our skies could turn grey and hazy too, and we may need to take precautions like staying indoors.

lenses.me: If haze reaches Singapore, you might need to stay indoors during recess or PE, and the sky could look grey and smoky.
lenses.family: Your family may need to check the NEA's air quality readings and keep N95 masks at home, especially for grandparents or family members with breathing problems.
lenses.friends: Outdoor sports and CCA training could be cancelled or moved indoors if the air becomes unhealthy, just like in past haze episodes.
lenses.nation: Singapore's government regularly talks to Indonesia about stopping the fires, since haze can affect our health, tourism and even flight schedules.
lenses.world: This shows how one country's actions — like burning forests to clear land — can affect the health and daily lives of people in nearby countries.

compo_words.example: The hazardous smoke made it difficult for residents to breathe outdoors.

stories.title: Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia Promise to Keep Busy Sea Routes Safe
stories.headline_kid: Three countries near Singapore have agreed to work together so ships can sail safely through some of the busiest waters in the world.
summary: The Malacca and Singapore Straits are narrow sea passages right next to Singapore. Thousands of ships pass through here every single day, carrying everything from oil to toys to your favourite snacks.

At a meeting called the 17th Cooperation Forum, Singapore's Transport Minister Jeffrey Siow said that recent events around the world have shown that safe sea routes cannot be 'taken for granted' — meaning we shouldn't assume they will always stay safe without effort.
Singapore, Malaysia and Indonesia agreed that keeping these waters safe and open depends on countries following international rules and working together, rather than acting alone.

This matters a lot for Singapore because we are a major port city. Much of what we eat, wear and use travels through these straits by ship, so keeping them safe helps keep prices stable and goods flowing smoothly.

lenses.me: Many things you use every day — your school shoes, snacks, even your phone parts — probably arrived in Singapore by ship through these straits.
lenses.family: If the straits become unsafe, ships might need to take longer routes, which could make things your family buys more expensive.
lenses.friends: Some of your friends' parents might work in shipping, ports or logistics — jobs that depend on these waters staying safe.
lenses.nation: Singapore's economy relies heavily on trade passing safely through the straits, since we are one of the world's busiest ports.
lenses.world: This shows how neighbouring countries can choose to cooperate instead of compete, to protect something that benefits everyone.

compo_words.example: The three ministers reaffirmed their commitment to keeping the waters safe.
Patrol ships help safeguard the busy shipping lane from pirates.
The strait is a vital route for global trade.

compo_phrases.example: We should not take safe sea routes for granted.

stories.title: More Days Off for Parents — But What About Everyone Else?
stories.headline_kid: Singapore wants to give parents more time off to care for their children — but some workers without kids worry they'll end up with extra work.
summary: At this year's National Day Rally, the government announced plans to give working parents more childcare leave — special paid days off to care for their children, such as when a child is sick or has a school event.
This is part of Singapore's bigger plan to encourage more people to have children, since our birth rate has been falling for years.

However, some workers who don't have children have raised a concern: when a colleague suddenly takes childcare leave at short notice, their extra work often falls onto someone else's plate — leaving less time for their own personal or family life.
Most people support helping parents, but the government now needs to find a fair way to share the extra workload so no one feels overworked or left out.

lenses.me: If your parents get more childcare leave, they might be able to be around more often when you're sick or have a school event.
lenses.family: Your parents may be able to spend more time with your family without losing income, but their colleagues might feel more pressure at work.
lenses.friends: Some friends may notice their parents picking them up from school more often or attending more school events.
lenses.nation: This is part of Singapore's push to raise its birth rate, since fewer babies are being born each year.
lenses.world: Many countries are facing the same falling birth rate problem, and they are watching how Singapore's approach works out.

compo_words.example: Singapore's low fertility rate is a concern for the government.
The government plans to extend childcare leave for working parents.

stories.title: Air India Asks Singapore Airlines and Tata for Big Money Help
stories.headline_kid: Air India needs about S$2 billion from its owners — including our own Singapore Airlines — after losing a lot of money.
summary: Singapore Airlines (SIA) doesn't just fly planes for Singapore — it also owns a share of Air India, one of India's biggest airlines, together with an Indian company called Tata Sons.

Air India has been losing large amounts of money recently, so it is now asking its owners for about US$1.5 billion (roughly S$2 billion) in fresh funding. This is called 'equity' — money that owners put into a company to help keep it running.
If this request goes through, it would be one of the biggest funding calls Air India has made since Tata took over the airline from the Indian government a few years ago.

This matters to Singapore because SIA is a major Singapore company. If SIA has to spend a lot of money helping Air India, it could affect SIA's own profits, which in turn can matter for jobs, investments and even how Singapore's economy performs.

lenses.me: If your family has flown with SIA or Air India before, this news shows how connected our national airline is to companies around the world.
lenses.family: Your family's flight bookings or holiday plans aren't likely to change immediately, but it shows how business decisions can ripple across borders.
lenses.friends: Friends whose parents work in the aviation or finance industry might be talking about this news at home.
lenses.nation: Singapore has big investments in aviation, showing how closely our economy is linked to businesses in other countries.
lenses.world: This shows the challenges many airlines around the world still face in trying to recover and grow their businesses.

stories.title: Japan's 'Human Fridge' Cools Down Workers in Scorching Heat
stories.headline_kid: Workers in Japan are stepping into a giant fridge-like box to cool off during extremely hot days — could hot, humid Singapore need one too?
summary: Japan has been having a punishing hot summer, and workers have been feeling dizzy and unwell from the extreme heat. One company in Osaka bought a special invention to help — a phonebooth-sized 'human fridge' that blasts icy-cold air onto tired, overheated workers.

It works a bit like stepping into a walk-in freezer, but designed just for people. Workers who feel unwell from the heat can step in for a few minutes to cool down quickly and safely before going back to work.
This shows how extreme heat, made worse by climate change, is becoming a real problem for workers all around the world — and how companies are inventing clever gadgets to keep people safe.

Singapore is hot and humid all year round too. While we may not need a 'human fridge' here, our National Environment Agency reminds everyone — especially outdoor workers, delivery riders and students playing sports — to drink water often and rest in the shade when it's very hot.

lenses.me: On very hot days after PE or games, remember to drink water and rest in the shade, just like these Japanese workers do in their cooling box.
lenses.family: Family members who work outdoors, like delivery riders, cleaners or construction workers, face similar heat challenges here in Singapore.
lenses.friends: Friends who play outdoor sports or CCAs need to remember to hydrate often, especially during Singapore's hot afternoons.
lenses.nation: Singapore has been reminding workplaces to take heat-safety seriously, since our weather is getting hotter due to climate change.
lenses.world: Extreme heat is becoming more common in many countries, pushing scientists and companies to invent creative solutions to keep people safe.
